HM-01.c01: **Hazardous materials** (HazMat, or HM) are products that can hurt people, harm health, or damage property while they are being moved.
**Shipper** = the business that sends and prepares the product; **carrier** = the company that moves it; consignee = who receives it.
A **label** is a small diamond on a package; a **placard** is a large diamond on the vehicle or bulk package showing the hazard class.
**Shipping paper** = any paper describing the HazMat, such as shipping orders, bills of lading and manifests.
**Reportable quantity (RQ)** = the amount of a listed hazardous substance that must be marked "RQ" and whose spill must be reported.
HM-01.c02: You need a **CDL with an "H" endorsement** to drive a HazMat vehicle of **any size**, and you must pass a knowledge test to get it.
A **CLP holder may not** haul HazMat.
The federal HazMat rules (HMR) are in **CFR, Title 49, Parts 171–180**.
The Hazardous Materials Table is **not complete**; whether something is HazMat depends on its properties and the **shipper's decision**.
[CA] DMV examiners will **not** give CDL skills tests in a vehicle showing **placards** (CVC §27903).
HM-01.c03: Your employer must train and test you at least **once every 3 years** and keep the record while you work with HazMat **plus 90 days**.
All drivers need **security** training; special training is needed for certain flammable gas, highway-route radioactive loads, and cargo or portable tanks.
A new or renewed "H" endorsement requires a **TSA** background check: fingerprints, a fee, and **1** ID document.
[CA] Motor carriers need a **CHP** HazMat license for placarded loads, or loads **over 500 lb** hauled for a fee that would need placards in larger amounts; carry a copy in the vehicle.
[CA] For permits or routes contact CHP and DOT; hazardous waste → **Department of Toxic Substances Control**; medical waste → Department of Health Services.
HM-01.c04: The rules have 3 goals: **contain** the material, **communicate** the risk, and assure safe drivers and equipment.
Packaging rules are **containment rules**; labels, shipping papers, emergency response information and **placards** communicate the risk.
To pass the test, know how to **identify** HazMat, load it safely, placard correctly and transport it safely.
Breaking the rules can bring **fines and jail**; inspect your vehicle **before and during each trip**, since officers may check papers, placards and your endorsement.
HM-01.c05: The **shipper** packages, marks and labels the HazMat, prepares the shipping papers, gives emergency response information, supplies placards and **certifies** the load.
The **carrier** checks that the shipment was prepared correctly **before** moving it and refuses improper shipments.
The **driver** checks the load, **refuses leaking packages**, placards the vehicle at loading, and delivers it safely with no delays.
The driver keeps papers and emergency response information in place and **reports** any HazMat crash or incident while in control of the load.
HM-01.c06: There are **9 hazard classes**, such as 1 explosives, 2 gases, 3 flammable liquids, 7 radioactive and 8 corrosives; ORM-D and combustible liquids have no number.
Examples: **2.3** is poisonous gases, 4.3 is dangerous when wet, 6.2 is infectious substances; gasoline is Class 3, battery fluid Class 8.
Keep HazMat papers on **top** of other papers or clearly marked, with the emergency response information.
While driving, papers go in the **door pouch** or in clear view within reach while belted; when you leave the vehicle, **on the driver's seat**.
Shippers put **diamond-shaped** labels on most packages; if a label won't fit, they use a tag (cylinders get tags or decals).
HM-01.c07: Placards go on the outside of the vehicle and on bulk packages and show the **hazard class** of the cargo.
A placarded vehicle needs at least **4 identical placards** (front, rear, both sides), readable from all 4 directions.
Placards are at least **9.84 inches (250 mm)** square, turned square-on-point; bulk packages show ID numbers on placards, orange panels or white diamonds.
An **ID number** has **4 digits**, follows "UN" or "NA", and may cover more than 1 chemical; the ERG lists them.
Check **3 lists**: the Hazardous Materials Table, Appendix A (hazardous substances and RQs) and Appendix B (marine pollutants).
HM-01.c08: Column 1 has **6** symbols: + (use the name even if the class definition isn't met), A air, W water, D domestic, I international, G generic.
A **G** name must be followed by a **technical name**; proper shipping names are in regular type, never italics.
Column 3 gives the class or "**Forbidden**" (never haul it); placards depend on class, amount shipped and total HazMat on the vehicle.
Column 4 ID numbers follow UN, NA or ID (**NA** = U.S. and to/from Canada only); Column 5 is the packing group in Roman numerals.
Column 7 numbers **1–6** = **poison inhalation hazard**; Column 8 is the 3-part packaging column; Columns 9 and 10 don't apply to highway.
HM-01.c09: Appendix A lists each hazardous substance's **reportable quantity (RQ)**, such as phosgene 10 lb, phosphine 100 lb, phosphoric acid 5,000 lb.
When **1 package** holds the RQ or more, the shipper shows "RQ" on the paper and package; you or your employer must **report** such spills.
INHALATION HAZARD on the paper or package → **POISON INHALATION HAZARD** or POISON GAS placards plus class placards, **even for small amounts**.
On the highway, the marine pollutant list is used only for containers of **119 gallons or more** without HMR placards or labels.
Bulk marine pollutants show a **white triangle with a crossed-out fish**: a marking, not a placard, also shown on the vehicle; the paper says MARINE POLLUTANT.
HM-01.c10: A multi-page paper shows the total on page 1, like **"Page 1 of 4"**, and needs a proper description for each HazMat and a signed shipper's certification.
On a mixed paper, HazMat is **listed first**, highlighted in a contrasting color, or marked "X" (or "RQ") in an **HM** column.
Basic description order: **ID number, proper shipping name, hazard class, packing group** (UN1263, Paint, 3, PG II); hazardous waste adds **WASTE** before the name.
The **shipper** provides the emergency response phone number and information (at least **7** kinds of facts); the driver gives it to responding officials.
The shipper keeps papers **2 years** (**3 years** for hazardous waste); a carrier that only provides carrier service keeps a copy 1 year.
HM-01.c11: The shipper signs a **certification** on the original shipping paper that the load was prepared by the HMR.
Exceptions: a **private carrier** hauling its own product, and when the carrier supplies the package, such as a **cargo tank**.
You may **accept** the shipper's certification unless a package is **clearly unsafe** or does not follow the HMR; also follow your employer's rules.
